title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E01.Q01
text:
Question: What is the role of a prototype program in problem solving?

Instructor answer: To simulate the behaviour of portions of the desired software product.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E01.Q02
text:
Question: What stages in the software life cycle are influenced by the testing stage?

Instructor answer: The testing stage can influence both the coding stage (phase 5) and the solution refinement stage (phase 7)

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E01.Q03
text:
Question: What are the main advantages associated with object-oriented programming?

Instructor answer: Abstraction and reusability.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E01.Q04
text:
Question: Where do C++ programs begin to execute?

Instructor answer: At the main function.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E01.Q05
text:
Question: What is a variable?

Instructor answer: A location in memory that can store a value.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E01.Q06
text:
Question: Where are variables declared in a C++ program?

Instructor answer: Variables can be declared anywhere in a program. They can be declared inside a function (local variables) or outside the functions (global variables)

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E01.Q07
text:
Question: What is the main difference between a while and a do ... while statement?

Instructor answer: The block inside a do ... while statement will execute at least once.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E02.Q01
text:
Question: What is typically included in a class definition?

Instructor answer: Data members (attributes) and member functions.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E02.Q02
text:
Question: What is the difference between a data member and a local variable inside a member function?

Instructor answer: Data members can be accessed from any member functions inside the class defintion. Local variables can only be accessed inside the member function that defines them.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E02.Q03
text:
Question: What is the difference between a constructor and a function?

Instructor answer: A constructor is called whenever an object is created, whereas a function needs to be called explicitely. Constructors do not have return type, but functions have to indicate a return type.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E02.Q04
text:
Question: When does C++ create a default constructor?

Instructor answer: If no constructor is provided, the compiler provides one by default. If a constructor is defined for a class, the compiler does not create a default constructor.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E02.Q05
text:
Question: How many constructors can be created for a class?

Instructor answer: Unlimited number.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E02.Q06
text:
Question: What is the difference between a function prototype and a function definition?

Instructor answer: A function prototype includes the function signature, i.e., the name of the function, the return type, and the parameters's type. The function definition includes the actual body of the function.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E02.Q07
text:
Question: What is the role of a header-file?

Instructor answer: To store a class interface, including data members and member function prototypes.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E03.Q01
text:
Question: What does a function signature include?

Instructor answer: The name of the function and the types of the parameters.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E03.Q02
text:
Question: What is the scope of global variables?

Instructor answer: File scope.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E03.Q03
text:
Question: How does the compiler handle inline functions?

Instructor answer: It makes a copy of the function code in every place where a function call is made.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E03.Q04
text:
Question: What is the main advantage associated with function arguments that are passed by reference?

Instructor answer: It avoids making copies of large data structures when calling functions.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E03.Q05
text:
Question: How are overloaded functions differentiated by the compiler?

Instructor answer: Based on the function signature. When an overloaded function is called, the compiler will find the function whose signature is closest to the given function call.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E03.Q06
text:
Question: When defining a recursive function, what are possible causes for infinite recursion?

Instructor answer: If the recursion step is defined incorrectly, or if the base case is not included.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E03.Q07
text:
Question: What are the similarities between iteration and recursion?

Instructor answer: They both involve repetition; they both have termination tests; they can both occur infinitely.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E04.Q01
text:
Question: What are the two different ways of specifying the length of an array?

Instructor answer: In the array declaration, or by using an initializer list.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E04.Q02
text:
Question: What is the main difference between strings declared using the type string versus strings declared using an array of characters?

Instructor answer: The strings declared using an array of characters have a null element added at the end of the array.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E04.Q03
text:
Question: How are arrays passed to functions?

Instructor answer: by reference.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E04.Q04
text:
Question: What is the difference between an array declared as static, and one that is not?

Instructor answer: The arrays declared as static live throughout the life of the program; that is, they are initialized only once, when the function that declares the array it is first called.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E04.Q05
text:
Question: How many dimensions need to be specified when passing a multi-dimensional array as an argument to a function?

Instructor answer: All the dimensions, except the first one.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E05.Q01
text:
Question: In one sentence, what is the main idea implemented by insertion sort?

Instructor answer: Taking one array element at a time, from left to right, it inserts it in the right position among the already sorted elements on its left.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E05.Q02
text:
Question: In one sentence, what is the main idea implemented by selection sort?

Instructor answer: Taking one array element at a time, from left to right, it identifies the minimum from the remaining elements and swaps it with the current element.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E05.Q03
text:
Question: What is the number of operations for insertion sort under a best-case scenario, and what is the best-case scenario?

Instructor answer: N (the length of the array) operations achieved for a sorted array.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E05.Q04
text:
Question: What is the base case for a recursive implementation of merge sort?

Instructor answer: When the size of the array to be sorted is 1 (or 2)

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E06.Q01
text:
Question: What is a pointer?

Instructor answer: A variable that contains the address in memory of another variable.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E06.Q02
text:
Question: What does the address (&) operator return?

Instructor answer: The memory address of its operand.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E06.Q03
text:
Question: What does the star (*) operator return?

Instructor answer: An alias (synonym) for the name of the object that its operand points to in memory. It is the dereferencing operator.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E06.Q04
text:
Question: How can an array be addressed in pointer or offset notation?

Instructor answer: By initializing a pointer to point to the first element of the array, and then incrementing this pointer with the index of the array element.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E06.Q05
text:
Question: What does the sizeof operator return?

Instructor answer: The size in bytes of its operand.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E06.Q06
text:
Question: What are the different ways to pass a pointer to a function?

Instructor answer: There are four ways: nonconstant pointer to constant data, nonconstant pointer to nonconstant data, constant pointer to constant data, constant pointer to nonconstant data.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E06.Q07
text:
Question: What is a function pointer?

Instructor answer: The address of the location in memory where the function code resides.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E07.Q01
text:
Question: What is a linked list?

Instructor answer: A collection of elements that can be allocated dynamically.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E07.Q02
text:
Question: What is the main advantage of linked lists over arrays?

Instructor answer: The linked lists can be of variable length.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E07.Q03
text:
Question: What is the main advantage of arrays over linked lists?

Instructor answer: The elements in an array can be accessed directly (as opposed to linked lists, which require iterative traversal).

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E07.Q04
text:
Question: How are linked lists passed as arguments to a function?

Instructor answer: By reference.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E07.Q05
text:
Question: What is the difference between a circular linked list and a basic linked list?

Instructor answer: The last element in a circular linked list points to the head of the list.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E07.Q06
text:
Question: What is the main advantage of a doubly-linked list over a basic linked list?

Instructor answer: All the deletion and insertion operations can be performed in constant time, including those operations performed before a given location in the list or at the end of the list.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E07.Q07
text:
Question: What is the main disadvantage of a doubly-linked list over a basic linked list?

Instructor answer: Extra space required to store the back pointers.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E08.Q01
text:
Question: What is a stack?

Instructor answer: A data structure that can store elements, which has the property that the last item added will be the first to be removed (or last-in-first-out)

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E08.Q02
text:
Question: What are the two main functions defined by a stack?

Instructor answer: push and pop

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E08.Q03
text:
Question: How can you implement a stack with an array?

Instructor answer: Keep the top of the stack toward the end of the array, so the push and pop operations will add or remove elements from the right side of the array.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E08.Q04
text:
Question: How can you implement a stack with a list?

Instructor answer: Keep the top of the stack pointing to the head of the linked list, so the push and pop operations will add or remove elements at the beginning of the list.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E08.Q06
text:
Question: How are infix expressions evaluated by computers?

Instructor answer: First, they are converted into postfix form, followed by an evaluation of the postfix expression.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E08.Q07
text:
Question: What operations would you need to perform to find a given element on a stack?

Instructor answer: Pop all the elements and store them on another stack until the element is found, then push back all the elements on the original stack.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E09.Q01
text:
Question: What is a queue?

Instructor answer: A data structure that can store elements, which has the property that the last item added will be the last to be removed (or first-in-first-out).

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E09.Q02
text:
Question: What are the two main functions defined by a queue?

Instructor answer: enqueue and dequeue

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E09.Q03
text:
Question: How can you implement a queue with an array?

Instructor answer: Use a circular array. Keep the rear of the queue toward the end of the array, and the front toward the beginning, and allow the rear pointer to wrap around.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E09.Q04
text:
Question: How can you implement a queue with a list?

Instructor answer: Keep the rear of the queue pointing to the tail of the linked list, so the enqueue operation is done at the end of the list, and keep the front of the queue pointing to the head of the linked list, so the dequeue operation is done at the beginning of the list.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E09.Q06
text:
Question: What is the stack operation corresponding to the enqueue operation in queues?

Instructor answer: push

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E10.Q01
text:
Question: What is a tree?

Instructor answer: A collection of nodes, which has a special node called root, and the rest of the nodes are partitioned into one or more disjoint sets, each set being a tree.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E10.Q02
text:
Question: What is the height of a tree?

Instructor answer: The length of the longest path from the root to any of its leaves.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E10.Q03
text:
Question: What is a leaf?

Instructor answer: A node that has no children.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E10.Q04
text:
Question: What is a binary tree?

Instructor answer: A tree for which the maximum number of children per node is two.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E10.Q05
text:
Question: What is a binary search tree?

Instructor answer: A binary tree that has the property that for any node the left child is smaller than the parent which in turn is smaller than the right child.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E10.Q06
text:
Question: What is the inorder traversal of a binary tree?

Instructor answer: Traverse the left subtree, then the root, then the right subtree.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E10.Q07
text:
Question: How many comparisons does it take to find an element in a binary search tree?

Instructor answer: The height of the tree (or log of the number of elements in the tree).

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E11.Q01
text:
Question: What are the elements typically included in a class definition?

Instructor answer: Function members and data members.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E11.Q02
text:
Question: What are the access-specifiers that can be used in a C++ class definition?

Instructor answer: Private and public.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E11.Q03
text:
Question: How are objects initialized when they are created?

Instructor answer: By using constructors.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E11.Q04
text:
Question: What is a function signature?

Instructor answer: The name of the function and the list of parameters, including their types.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E11.Q05
text:
Question: What is a recursive function?

Instructor answer: A function that calls itself.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E11.Q06
text:
Question: What is the alternative way to solve a problem that could be solved through recursive functions?

Instructor answer: Through iteration.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E11.Q07
text:
Question: What is the difference between an array that is declared as static and one that is not?

Instructor answer: The static arrays are intialized only once when the function is called.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E11.Q08
text:
Question: What is the main difference between a string of characters that is read into a variable of type string versus a variable of type char []?

Instructor answer: The char [] will automatically add a null 0 character at the end of the string.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E11.Q09
text:
Question: Briefly describe the divide-and-conquer paradigm.

Instructor answer: Divide a problem into smaller subproblems, solve them recursively, and then combine the solutions into a solution for the original problem.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E11.Q10
text:
Question: Briefly describe in one sentence how does merge sort work?

Instructor answer: It splits the original array into two, sorts each of the two halves, and then merges the sorted arrays.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E12.Q01
text:
Question: What is a pointer?

Instructor answer: The address of a location in memory.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E12.Q02
text:
Question: What is the experimental approach for measuring the running time of an algorithm?

Instructor answer: Implement the algorithm and measure the physical running time.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E12.Q04
text:
Question: Briefly, how does selection sort work?

Instructor answer: It selects the minimum from an array and places it on the first position, then it selects the minimum from the rest of the array and places it on the second position, and so forth.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E12.Q05
text:
Question: What is the advantage of linked lists over arrays?

Instructor answer: Linked lists are dynamic structures, which allow for a variable number of elements to be stored.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E12.Q06
text:
Question: What is a queue?

Instructor answer: A data structure that stores elements following the first in first out principle. The main operations in a queue are enqueue and dequeue.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E12.Q07
text:
Question: What are the main operations associated with a stack?

Instructor answer: push and pop

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E12.Q08
text:
Question: What is the Euler tour traversal of a tree?

Instructor answer: A walk around the tree, starting with the root, where each node is seen three times: from the left, from below, from the right.

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E12.Q09
text:
Question: How do you delete a node from a binary search tree?

Instructor answer: Find the node, then replace it with the leftmost node from its right subtree (or the rightmost node from its left subtree).

title: Instructor reference answers
heading: E12.Q10
text:
Question: How many steps does it take to search a node in a binary search tree?

Instructor answer: The height of the tree.

title: Course notes: Algorithm analysis
heading: Counting operations
text:
There are two ways to find out how long an algorithm takes. The experimental approach is to implement the algorithm and measure the physical running time. It gives real numbers, but they depend on the machine, the compiler, the inputs that were tried and whatever else the computer was doing, and it needs a finished program.

The analytic approach, which we use for the rest of the course, is to count the basic operations that the algorithm performs, as a function of the size of its input. The input size is written n or N: the length of the array, or the number of nodes in the list or tree. A basic operation is one that takes a fixed amount of time whatever n is: comparing two elements, copying one element, following one pointer, one arithmetic operation.

For sorting and searching we usually count the comparisons between elements, and sometimes also the moves (copies or swaps), because these dominate the running time. Everything else the algorithm does happens at most a fixed number of times per comparison.

Counting gives a formula in n, such as n - 1 or n(n - 1)/2. We then keep only how the formula grows as n becomes large, which is what Big-O notation records.

title: Course notes: Algorithm analysis
heading: Best case, average case and worst case
text:
For most algorithms the number of operations depends not only on how many elements there are but also on which elements they are and how they are arranged. A linear search for a value in an array of n elements may stop at the first element, or it may have to look at all n. So we describe an algorithm with three functions of n.

The worst case is the largest number of operations over all inputs of size n. It is a guarantee: the algorithm never does more work than this.

The best case is the smallest number of operations over all inputs of size n.

The average case is the expected number of operations over all inputs of size n, under an assumption about how likely each input is. The usual assumption is that every arrangement is equally likely.

For linear search in an array of n elements: the best case is 1 comparison (the value is in the first position), the worst case is n comparisons (the value is in the last position or is absent), and the average case is about n/2 comparisons when the value is present.

Each of the three is a statement about inputs of the same size n. Whenever you give a count, say which case it belongs to and which input produces it. Quoting the worst-case formula as the best case, or the reverse, is a common slip.

title: Course notes: Algorithm analysis
heading: Best case means best arrangement, not smallest input
text:
All three cases are defined for the same input size n. The best case is the most favourable arrangement of n elements. It is not the smallest input.

Asking for the best case of a sorting algorithm does not mean asking what happens for an array of one or two elements. Every algorithm is fast on a tiny input, so that would say nothing about the algorithm. The size n stays general, and we ask which of the possible arrays of length n makes the algorithm do the least work.

For insertion sort the most favourable arrangement is an array that is already sorted: each element is compared with its left neighbour once and stays where it is, which gives N operations for an array of length N. For linear search it is an array in which the value being looked for happens to come first. For selection sort and merge sort the arrangement makes no difference to the order of growth, so their best case and worst case are of the same order.

A useful check: a best-case count is still an expression in n, such as n or n log n. A count of exactly 1 operation is a best case only for an algorithm that really can stop after one step on an arbitrarily large input, as linear search can. A sort cannot, because it has to look at every element at least once.

title: Course notes: Algorithm analysis
heading: Asymptotic notation
text:
Big-O notation describes how an operation count grows as n grows, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. We say that f(n) is O(g(n)) if, for all sufficiently large n, f(n) is at most a constant multiple of g(n). So 3n + 5 is O(n). The count n(n - 1)/2 equals n^2/2 - n/2 and is O(n^2): the n^2 term dominates as n grows, and the factor one half is dropped.

The growth rates we meet in this course, from the slowest growing to the fastest, are O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n), O(n^2) quadratic and O(2^n) exponential. For n equal to one million, log n is about 20, n log n is about twenty million, and n^2 is a million million.

Logarithms in this course are to base 2 unless we say otherwise: log n is the number of times n can be halved before it reaches 1. Logarithms to different bases differ only by a constant factor, so the base does not matter inside a Big-O.

Big-O is an upper bound on growth, and it can be applied to any of the three cases. It is correct to say that the worst case of insertion sort is O(n^2) and that its best case is O(n). Big-O does not by itself mean worst case, although a bound given without naming the case is normally read as the worst case.

title: Course notes: Algorithm analysis
heading: The cost of insertion sort
text:
Insertion sort takes one array element at a time, from left to right, and inserts it in the right position among the already sorted elements on its left. To insert an element it compares the element with its left neighbours one at a time, shifting each larger neighbour one position to the right, until it meets a neighbour that is not larger or reaches the start of the array.

Best case. The number of operations for insertion sort under a best-case scenario is N, the length of the array, and the best-case scenario is an array that is already sorted. Each element then needs a single comparison with its left neighbour and no shifting. Strictly that is N - 1 comparisons, because the first element has no left neighbour. In this course we state the count as N operations, which is O(n).

Worst case. The array is in reverse order. The element at position i is compared with, and shifted past, all i elements on its left, for a total of 1 + 2 + ... + (N - 1) = N(N - 1)/2 comparisons, which is O(n^2).

Average case. In a random arrangement each element travels about halfway back, which gives about N^2/4 comparisons, also O(n^2).

So N belongs to the best case and N(N - 1)/2 belongs to the worst case. Of the sorting algorithms in this course, insertion sort is the one whose cost depends most on how the input is arranged.

title: Course notes: Algorithm analysis
heading: The cost of selection sort
text:
Selection sort takes one array element at a time, from left to right, identifies the minimum from the remaining elements and swaps it with the current element. Put another way, it selects the minimum from the array and places it in the first position, then selects the minimum from the rest of the array and places it in the second position, and so forth.

Finding the minimum of the remaining elements means looking at every one of them. There is no way to stop early. The first pass makes N - 1 comparisons, the second N - 2, and so on down to 1, for a total of N(N - 1)/2 comparisons, which is O(n^2).

This count does not depend on the arrangement of the input. A sorted array, a reversed array and a random array of length N all cost exactly N(N - 1)/2 comparisons, so the best case, the average case and the worst case of selection sort are all O(n^2). Only the number of swaps varies, and it is never more than N - 1, one per pass. That is why selection sort is sometimes chosen when moving an element is expensive.

Compare this with insertion sort, which needs only N operations on a sorted array. Being sorted already helps insertion sort and does not help selection sort.

title: Course notes: Algorithm analysis
heading: The cost of merge sort
text:
Merge sort splits the array into two halves, sorts each half recursively, and merges the two sorted halves. Its cost follows from the shape of the recursion.

Each level of the recursion handles all n elements once. At the top level one merge combines two halves of n/2 elements. At the next level two merges combine four quarters, and so on. Merging sorted pieces that hold n elements in total takes at most n - 1 comparisons, so every level costs about n operations.

The number of levels is the number of times n can be halved before the pieces reach base-case size, which is log n. The total is about n operations per level times log n levels: merge sort is O(n log n).

Unlike insertion sort, merge sort does this much work whatever the arrangement of the input, because it always splits in the middle and always merges at every level. Its best case, average case and worst case are all O(n log n). The exact number of comparisons in a merge varies a little with the data, but the order of growth does not.

The price is memory. Merging needs a temporary array of n elements, whereas insertion sort and selection sort sort the array in place. For large arrays merge sort is still far faster: for a million elements, n log n is about twenty million operations and n^2 is a million million.

title: Course notes: Algorithm analysis
heading: Searching a binary search tree: the cost is the height
text:
A binary search tree is a binary tree in which, for any node, the left child is smaller than the parent, which in turn is smaller than the right child. The same holds for everything in the node's left and right subtrees.

To search for a key, start at the root and compare the key with the value in the node. If they are equal, the search is finished. If the key is smaller, continue in the left subtree; if it is larger, in the right subtree. An empty subtree means the key is not in the tree.

Each comparison moves the search one level down, and the other subtree is never looked at. The search therefore follows a single path from the root towards a leaf, and cannot examine more nodes than the longest such path contains. The height of a tree is the length of the longest path from the root to any of its leaves.

In this course the answer to how many comparisons, or how many steps, it takes to find an element in a binary search tree is the height of the tree. It can also be given as the log of the number of elements in the tree, which is the height when the tree is balanced. Counting the root, a search can examine one node more than the height. We ignore that difference: the cost grows with the height of the tree, not with the number of nodes.

title: Course notes: Algorithm analysis
heading: Balanced and degenerate trees
text:
How large the height is depends on the shape of the tree, and the shape depends on the order in which the keys were inserted.

A balanced tree is as short as it can be: every level is full, except possibly the last. Level k of a binary tree holds up to 2^k nodes, so a tree with n nodes needs only about log n levels. The height of a balanced tree with n nodes is about log n. A balanced tree with 1,000 nodes has height 9, and one with a million nodes has height 19. Searching a balanced binary search tree is O(log n).

A degenerate tree is as tall as it can be: every node has only one child, so the tree is a chain. This is what a binary search tree turns into when the keys are inserted in sorted order. Its height is n - 1, and a search may have to pass through every node, exactly as in a linked list. Searching a degenerate binary search tree is O(n).

The complete statement is therefore this. Searching a binary search tree takes a number of steps equal to the height of the tree, which is about log n for the best shape, a balanced tree, and n - 1 for the worst shape, a degenerate tree. When we quote log n for a binary search tree we are assuming that the tree is balanced. A cost of n belongs only to the degenerate tree.

title: Course notes: Algorithm analysis
heading: Linear scan versus tree search
text:
It helps to put the searches we know side by side, for a collection of n elements.

Linear scan of an unsorted array or of a linked list. Each comparison eliminates one element. The worst case is n comparisons, and the average is about n/2 when the element is present. O(n).

Binary search of a sorted array. Each comparison eliminates half of the remaining elements. At most about log n comparisons. O(log n).

Search in a balanced binary search tree. Each comparison eliminates one whole subtree, about half of the remaining nodes. At most about log n comparisons, the height of the tree. O(log n).

Counts such as n, n - 1 or n/2 are linear-scan counts. They describe looking at all of the elements, or at half of them. A search in a binary search tree does not visit every node, or half of the nodes, because every comparison discards a subtree without looking inside it. Visiting every node is what a traversal does (inorder, preorder or postorder), and a traversal is O(n).

Nor is n log n the cost of a search. O(n log n) is the cost of sorting n elements with merge sort, or of building a balanced tree by n insertions that cost O(log n) each. One search is a single path from the root towards a leaf: the height of the tree, which is O(log n) when the tree is balanced.

heading: Base case and recursive step
text:
The base case is the instance of the problem that the function can answer directly, without calling itself. For factorial it is n <= 1. For a search in a linked list it is the empty list. For a recursive sort it is an array so small that it needs no further splitting. A function may have more than one base case.

The recursive step, also called the recursion step or the recursive case, does three things. It makes the problem smaller, it calls the function on the smaller problem, and it uses the result of that call to finish the original problem. In factorial the smaller problem is n - 1 and the remaining work is one multiplication.

When you design a recursive function, write down both parts in words before writing any code. What is the smallest input, and what is the answer for it? For any larger input, which smaller input do I call the function on, and what do I do with what comes back?

The base case is usually written as an if statement at the top of the function, but that is a habit and not a rule. The test can be written the other way round, with the recursive call inside the if and nothing at all in the base case, as in a function that prints a list only while the list is not empty. What matters is that at least one path through the function makes no recursive call.

title: Course notes: Recursion
heading: Convergence: the step must move toward the base case
text:
Having a base case is not enough. Each recursive call must be made on an instance that is closer to a base case than the one before it, so that the chain of calls is certain to arrive there. We say that the recursion converges on the base case. The call factorial(n - 1) converges because the argument decreases by one on every call and must reach 1. A recursive binary search converges because the range between first and last shrinks on every call.

To check convergence, ask two questions about every recursive call. Which quantity measures the size of the problem: the value of n, the length of the array section, the height of the subtree? Does that quantity get strictly smaller on every call, and can it step over the base case without landing on it?

A step of n - 2 with the single base case n == 0 gets smaller every time, but it steps over zero whenever n is odd, so the base case is never reached. A call that passes the same argument again, or a larger one, never gets closer at all.

A base case that cannot be reached is as good as no base case. The test is there in the text of the function, but it never succeeds, and the calls continue.

title: Course notes: Recursion
heading: Causes of infinite recursion
text:
Infinite recursion means that the chain of recursive calls never ends. In this course we name two possible causes. Infinite recursion occurs if the recursion step is defined incorrectly, or if the base case is not included.

The base case is not included. The function has no path that returns without calling itself, so every call makes another call.

The recursion step is defined incorrectly. A base case exists, but the calls do not converge on it. The argument is not reduced (factorial(n) calls factorial(n)), or it moves in the wrong direction (n + 1 where n - 1 was meant), or it jumps past the base case (n - 2 when the test is n == 0 and n is odd).

In C++ an infinite recursion does not literally run forever. Every call that has not yet returned keeps a frame on the call stack, so the stack grows with each call until the program runs out of stack memory and is terminated, usually with a stack overflow or a segmentation fault. An infinite loop uses no additional memory per repetition and simply keeps running. The underlying error is the same in both: the test that should end the repetition is missing or can never succeed.

title: Course notes: Recursion
heading: The call stack: one frame per call
text:
Each call of a function, recursive or not, gets its own activation record, or stack frame, on the program's call stack. The frame holds that call's parameters, its local variables and the place in the caller to return to. When a function calls itself, a new frame is pushed on top of the caller's frame. The caller is not finished. It is suspended, with its own values intact, until the call it made returns.

Because each call has its own frame, each call has its own copy of the parameters and local variables. During factorial(3) there are, at the deepest point, three frames on the stack, with n equal to 3, 2 and 1. Changing n in one frame does not affect the others. A local variable declared inside a recursive function is created again for every call. It is not shared between the calls and it does not accumulate across them. To carry information from one call to the next, pass it as an argument or hand it back as the return value.

The depth of the recursion is the largest number of frames on the stack at one time. Memory use grows with the depth, which is why a very deep recursion can overflow the stack even when it is not infinite.

title: Course notes: Recursion
heading: What happens after a recursive call returns
text:
A recursive call is an ordinary function call. When it returns, execution continues in the caller at the point just after the call, with the caller's own parameters and local variables, and the statements that follow the call are then executed.

```cpp
void printUp(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return;     // base case
    printUp(n - 1);         // recursive call
    cout << n << ' ';       // runs after the call above has returned
}
```

The call printUp(3) prints 1 2 3. The calls go all the way down to n == 0 first. The output statements then run in the reverse order of the calls, as the frames are popped one by one. This is called unwinding the recursion. Moving the output statement in front of the recursive call would print 3 2 1 instead.

Reaching the base case therefore does not end the computation. The base case returns to the call that made it, that call finishes its remaining work and returns to its own caller, and so on back to the original call. In factorial every multiplication is performed during the unwinding: factorial(1) returns 1 to factorial(2), which returns 2 to factorial(3), which returns 6.

A function that produces a value must return the result of its recursive call, as in return n * factorial(n - 1). A void function such as printUp just makes the call.

title: Course notes: Recursion
heading: Iteration and recursion: the similarities
text:
Iteration and recursion are two ways of repeating work. In this course we list three similarities between them.

They both involve repetition. Iteration repeats the body of a loop. Recursion repeats the body of a function through repeated function calls.

They both have termination tests. Iteration ends when the loop-continuation condition fails. Recursion ends when a base case is recognized. In both, each repetition is supposed to bring the computation closer to the point where the test succeeds: a loop changes its control variable until the condition fails, and a recursion makes its problem smaller until it reaches the base case.

They can both occur infinitely. A loop whose condition never becomes false is an infinite loop. A recursion whose step does not converge on the base case, or that has no base case, is an infinite recursion.

These are the three similarities expected in this course: repetition, a termination test, and the possibility of running without end.

It is also true that the two are equally powerful. Any problem that can be solved recursively can be solved iteratively, and the reverse, although one of the two is often much clearer than the other.

title: Course notes: Recursion
heading: Iteration and recursion: the differences
text:
The two differ in mechanism and in cost. Iteration uses a repetition statement (for, while, do ... while) and keeps its state in variables that are updated in place. Recursion uses a selection statement, the test for the base case, together with function calls, and keeps its state in the parameters and local variables of each call.

Recursion has an overhead that iteration does not have. Every recursive call pushes a new frame on the call stack. That costs time for the call and memory for the frame, and the memory is held until the call returns. A loop that runs n times uses the same few variables throughout. A recursion that is n calls deep uses n frames. For this reason a simple count or accumulation, such as summing an array or computing a factorial, is normally written as a loop in production code.

Recursion is preferred when it mirrors the problem: processing a tree, where each subtree is a smaller tree, or a divide-and-conquer algorithm such as merge sort, where each half is a smaller array. A recursive solution can always be rewritten with iteration, sometimes with an explicit stack that takes the place of the call stack, so the choice between them is about clarity and cost and not about what can be computed.

title: Course notes: Recursion
heading: The divide-and-conquer paradigm
text:
Divide and conquer is an algorithm design paradigm with three steps. Divide a problem into smaller subproblems, solve them recursively, and then combine the solutions into a solution for the original problem.

Divide. Split the instance into smaller instances of the same problem, for example the two halves of an array.

Conquer. Solve each smaller instance by a recursive call. An instance small enough to be a base case is solved directly.

Combine. Put the solutions of the subproblems together, for example by merging two sorted halves into one sorted array.

Two things define the paradigm. The subproblems are the same kind of problem as the original, only smaller, which is why the same function can be called on them. And there is a combine step that builds the answer to the original problem out of the answers to the subproblems. Merge sort, quicksort and binary search all follow this pattern. In binary search only one of the two subproblems is kept and the combine step is trivial.

In this course the term means this recursive pattern. Splitting a large program into functions, classes or files, so that each piece is easier to write and to manage, is modular design. It is good practice and is sometimes described with the same words, but its pieces are different tasks and not smaller instances of one problem, and nothing is solved recursively.
